Experienced Grand Junction Personal Injury Lawyers

Grand Junction sits at the crossroads of I-70, US-50, and US-6, making it the primary transportation hub of Colorado’s Western Slope. Oil and gas industry traffic, agricultural trucking, and hundreds of thousands of annual visitors pass through Mesa County every year, and serious accidents happen regularly across the Grand Valley as a result. Navigating a personal injury claim in this environment requires attorneys who understand how to investigate Mesa County crashes, build cases for the 21st Judicial District, and stand up to insurance companies that expect injured people to accept whatever they offer first.

Our legal team brings the resources and trial experience of a Denver-based firm directly to injured clients on the Western Slope. We handle every case with the same level of attention, regardless of location, and we are prepared to litigate in Mesa County courts when a fair settlement is not on the table. Every client reaches their attorney directly, not a call center.

Types of Grand Junction Personal Injury Cases We Handle

The Grand Valley presents a distinctive injury landscape. High-speed freight collisions on I-70 through De Beque Canyon, motorcycle crashes on the roads leading to Colorado National Monument, and slip and fall incidents at commercial properties along Horizon Drive all reflect the region’s specific geography, traffic patterns, and local conditions.
At
Dormer Harpring
our attorneys handle a broad range of personal injury matters across Mesa County, including the following:
Car Accidents:
Collisions on I-70, US-6, and local Grand Junction roadways range from rear-end impacts at busy intersections to multi-vehicle pileups at highway speeds, often resulting in serious injuries.
Truck Accidents:
Freight carriers, oil field service trucks, and agricultural haulers share the roads throughout Mesa County, and crashes involving commercial vehicles tend to cause severe damage.
Motorcycle Accidents:
The canyon routes and open highways surrounding the Grand Valley attract riders year-round, and when a crash occurs, injuries are often significant.
Pedestrian Accidents:
Collisions along Horizon Drive and in Grand Junction’s downtown corridors can leave pedestrians with life-altering injuries and complex liability questions.
Premises Liability:
Property owners have a legal obligation to maintain safe conditions, and when they fail, slip and fall injuries can be far more serious than they first appear.
Dog Bites:
Colorado holds dog owners strictly liable for bite injuries, meaning the victim does not need to prove the owner knew the dog was dangerous.
Daycare Injuries:
When a childcare facility in Mesa County fails to provide adequate supervision or maintain safe conditions, the resulting harm to a child may give rise to a negligence claim against the facility.
Product Liability:
Defective vehicles, equipment, and consumer
products can cause injuries
without any driver error or negligence on the victim’s part.
Wrongful Death:
When a fatal accident leaves surviving family members without financial support or answers, a wrongful death claim can pursue accountability and compensation.
Every case type carries its own legal requirements, evidence standards, and deadlines. If the situation involves an injury not listed here, call
to find out how our
Grand Junction personal injury lawyers
can help.
Common Injuries in Grand Junction Personal Injury Cases

Not every injury looks serious at the scene. Some of the most consequential ones develop or worsen in the days following an accident, which is why a medical evaluation matters even when symptoms seem minor at first. The injuries most commonly seen in Mesa County cases include:
Traumatic brain injuries
, including concussions, are not always apparent right away
Spinal cord injuries
can result in lasting pain, limited mobility, or permanent paralysis
Broken bones and fractures frequently require surgery and extended recovery
Soft tissue injuries like
whiplash
are often undervalued by insurers
Burn injuries may require prolonged and costly medical treatment
Internal injuries can be life-threatening even when no outward symptoms appear
Seeking medical care right away protects both your health and the integrity of your claim, and creates a documented record that connects your injuries directly to the accident.
Who May Be Liable for Your Injuries in a Grand Junction Personal Injury Case

Personal injury liability in Colorado rarely falls on one party alone. Depending on how the accident occurred, responsibility may be shared across multiple individuals, companies, or entities, each carrying their own insurance coverage and legal exposure.
A
Grand Junction personal injury lawyer
can identify every potentially liable party before any statute of limitations runs out. Those parties may include:
Negligent drivers who ran a red light, drove impaired, or failed to yield
Trucking companies that pressured drivers to exceed hour limits, skipped maintenance, or hired unqualified drivers
Property owners who failed to address unsafe conditions like wet floors, broken staircases, or inadequate lighting
Product manufacturers, when a defective vehicle component or piece of equipment contributed to the injury
Government entities responsible for dangerous road design, failed traffic signals, or inadequate signage
Employers, when the at-fault driver was working at the time of the crash and acting within the scope of their employment
Identifying every liable party is one of the most important steps in a personal injury case. Missing one can mean leaving a significant source of compensation unclaimed.
Deadlines: How Long Do You Have to File an Injury Claim in Colorado?

Colorado sets strict deadlines for personal injury claims, and missing one almost always means permanently losing the right to recover compensation, regardless of how strong the case is. The deadline depends on the type of accident:
Car, truck, or motorcycle accidents carry a three-year filing deadline under
Slip and fall, dog bite, or general negligence claims must be filed within two years of the injury under
Wrongful death claims give surviving family members two years from the date of death under
Accidents involving a government entity require a formal notice within 182 days under
, separate from the standard filing deadline.

One detail worth knowing is Colorado’s discovery rule, which can shift the starting point of the deadline in cases where an injury was not immediately apparent. An injury diagnosed days or weeks after the accident may establish a different filing timeline.
If there is any uncertainty about which deadline applies, speaking with an attorney sooner rather than later is the safest step.
What to Do After an Accident in Grand Junction

The steps taken in the hours and days after an accident often determine what evidence survives, what injuries are properly documented, and how much leverage an injured person has when negotiations begin:
Seek medical attention right away, even when symptoms seem minor. St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center serves as the Grand Valley’s Level II trauma center for serious injuries.
Call law enforcement and request an official crash report documenting the scene, the parties involved, any citations issued, and the officer’s preliminary findings.
Photograph everything at the scene, including vehicle positions, road conditions, visible injuries, and the surrounding environment.
Collect witness information from anyone who observed the accident before they leave, including names, phone numbers, and a brief description of what they saw.
Avoid recorded statements to insurance adjusters until speaking with an attorney, as anything said early in the process can be used to minimize or deny a claim.
Contact a
Grand Junction personal injury lawyer
as early as possible so time-sensitive evidence, including vehicle data and surveillance footage, can be preserved.
The sooner these steps are taken, the stronger the foundation for a personal injury claim becomes.
What Compensation Can a Grand Junction Injury Claim Cover?
A
Grand Junction personal injury lawyer
can help identify every category of compensation available after an injury, which generally falls into three areas under Colorado law.
Economic Damages
Economic damages cover the measurable financial impact of an injury and form the foundation of most personal injury claims:
Medical expenses, including emergency care, hospitalization, surgery, and ongoing treatment
Future medical costs for long-term rehabilitation, therapy, or assistive care
Lost wages during recovery and reduced earning capacity for lasting impairments
Property damage, including vehicle repair or replacement costs
These losses are supported by documentation such as medical records, bills, and employment records, making them the most straightforward category to establish.
Non-Economic Damages

Some losses do not come with a bill or receipt. Colorado law allows injury victims to recover compensation for these personal losses too. Colorado law recognizes these losses as compensable, and Colorado’s non-economic damage cap was raised under
, which took effect January 1, 2025:
Physical pain and suffering resulting from the
trauma
of the injury and the recovery process that follows
Emotional distress and psychological trauma following the accident
Inconvenience caused by physical limitations and disruption to daily life
Reduced quality of life when an injury affects the ability to enjoy activities or relationships
Insurance companies often argue these losses are worth less than they really are. Strong evidence helps prove their value.
Punitive Damages

In cases where the defendant’s conduct was particularly reckless or willful, Colorado courts may award punitive damages in addition to compensatory damages. These awards are less common and require clear and convincing evidence of the defendant’s culpable state of mind, but they serve as an important accountability measure when egregious behavior is involved.
What If You Were Partly at Fault?
A common concern after an accident is whether sharing some responsibility means losing the right to compensation. Under Colorado law, that is not the case.
allows an injured person to recover damages as long as they were less than 50 percent at fault, with the total award reduced by their share of responsibility.

The bigger fight is usually over who caused the accident. Insurance companies often try to blame the injured person because it reduces the amount they have to pay. Those arguments are negotiating positions, not established facts, and they require evidence to push back against effectively. Anyone with questions about how shared fault might affect their claim is better served discussing the details with legal counsel than assuming recovery is off the table.

faqs.question: Will my personal injury case go to trial?

children.text: Most personal injury cases settle before trial. A trial may be necessary if the insurance company refuses to make a fair offer or denies responsibility for the accident.

faqs.question: How long does a personal injury case take?

children.text: Straightforward claims can be resolved in a matter of months. Cases involving serious injuries, disputed liability, or multiple parties often take one to two years or longer to reach a resolution.

faqs.question: How can I speed up my personal injury claim?

children.text: Gather your medical records early, follow your prescribed treatment plan, and respond to your attorney’s requests without delay.

faqs.question: How do I negotiate an insurance settlement?

children.text: Document every category of damages, respond to low offers in writing with supporting evidence, and work with a
Grand Junction personal injury lawyer
who can lead negotiations on your behalf.

faqs.question: What does a Grand Junction personal injury lawyer actually do for my case?

children.text: A personal injury lawyer investigates the accident, handles all communication with insurers, calculates the full value of your claim, and negotiates or litigates on your behalf so you are not left navigating the process alone.
